_metadata.scope: Ancestor levels above the item for Book I Distinction 37, Book II Distinction 44, and Book III Distinctions 23-25, together with partial Book I (including the Prologue item), Book II, Book III, and whole-work entries built from them.

alalal-z8229.summary: Distinction 37 of Book I treats God's presence in creatures, the places and motion of spirits, and divine immutability across thirty articles and three textual divisions. Albert holds that God is everywhere and in every thing because he conserves creation immediately; conservation cannot be delegated to any creature, and God's causality grounds rather than displaces the causality of creatures. God is in all things by essence, presence and power, which Albert traces to divine simplicity, subtlety and first causality. He is also in the saints by indwelling grace, which is a nobler presence that perfects the creature without changing God, and in Christ by union. Many articles refine the language of presence. 'In' is equivocal, so God contains the place he is 'in'. 'Everywhere' adds to 'in every thing' that God gives place its containing power, and it is the least improper of the related expressions. These predications connote temporal effects and so are not true of God from eternity. Omnipresence is proper to God alone, unlike the ubiquity of a universal. God is in himself, not nowhere; he is in the wicked only as to their nature; and he is not defiled, since he has no natural union, matter or position. Against this background the angels are treated as the contrasting case. They are in place definitively, through the limitation of their operation, not by circumscription. Two angels cannot share a place. Angels truly move, traversing space indivisibly by a power that overcomes distance, in three discrete nows rather than continuous or celestial time, and Aristotle's arguments against the motion of indivisibles do not apply to them. Being in place and being local are distinguished and applied analogically to God, spirits and bodies. Further articles establish that God is immobile, that he does not change by producing new effects, that knowledge is not numerically one across minds (against an Averroist reading), and that a thing is filled by God before it is filled by form or by place.
claims: God is everywhere and in every thing by essence, presence and power, conserving creation immediately without displacing created causality.
God is present in the saints by indwelling grace and in Christ by union, modes that perfect the creature without changing God.
When God is said to be 'in' a place, he contains it as its cause; omnipresence is proper to God and connotes temporal effects.
Angels are in place definitively through their limited operation, cannot share a place, and move locally in discrete instants by a power that overcomes distance.
God is immobile and immutable; new effects come from his eternal will.
Knowledge is not numerically one in different minds; the intelligible species is one as intention but many as an accident.

alalal-z15686.summary: Distinction 44, the last of Book II, closes the treatise on sin with the power of sinning and then turns to obedience and resistance to power. The power of sinning is a real power in its root, its essence and its relation to the substance of the act. With respect to the deformity of sin it is a defect and weakness yielding to malice. As a positive power it comes from God, while its ordering to evil comes from the creature's origin from nothing. The will alone commands sin, though many powers carry it out. On obedience, authority is never to be obeyed in commanding sin, since power is given for building up. Obedience owed in justice is limited by vow and office, while perfect obedience out of charity extends to every good. In conflicts, a higher authority prevails over one wholly derived from it, but coordinate authorities may have spheres the other cannot override. The devil must be resisted with all one's strength, and one should not want to be tempted. God-ordained power as such is not to be resisted, but the wicked will joined to it is. Usurped tyrannical power may be resisted as to obedience, though a tyranny permitted by God as a scourge must be endured.
claims: The power of sinning is a genuine power from God, while its ordering to evil comes from the creature's origin from nothing.
The will alone commands sin.
No authority is to be obeyed in commanding sin; obedience of justice is bounded by vow and office, perfect obedience by charity alone.
Ordained power must be obeyed, but usurped power and the devil's wicked will may be resisted, though divine scourges must be endured.
concepts: creation ex nihilo as source of defect

alalal-z19946.summary: Distinction 23 of Book III opens the treatise on faith by expounding Augustine's definition and that of Hebrews 11:1. Albert holds that faith is not a species of knowledge, because its assent is caused by the will rather than by evidence; in faith cognition is material and affection formal. Faith is a theological virtue residing in the 'affective intellect', ordered immediately to God, and its object is first truth held for its own sake. The believer first assents and then seeks reasons for delight and wonder, never resting on them. Faith is one because first truth underlies every article, though it is many materially. Believing God, believing that God is, and believing into God are three relations to this one object, and believing into God is faith working through love. Unformed faith is a virtue in a secondary sense. It becomes formed when grace and charity arrive rather than being replaced. Faith is formed by its own proper form, while grace makes its acts meritorious and charity orders them to the highest good. Demons have only a credulity resting on natural knowledge, located in the practical intellect. Faith concerns what is not apparent, because the articles conflict with the principles of natural reason. Its certainty is affective, coming from a light like first truth, and exceeds that of demonstration. One possesses one's own faith with certainty of acquaintance, but cannot thereby know with certainty that one is in grace. Hebrews 11:1 defines faith by its effects: it is the foundation of the spiritual building, making eternal goods subsist in us and convincing the mind through an infused, non-discursive light. Faith is the foundation in the strict sense and is naturally prior to hope and the other virtues.
claims: Faith is a theological virtue whose assent is caused by the will moved by first truth, not by evidence or reasoning.
Faith is one in its formal object, first truth, and many only materially in its articles.
Unformed faith becomes formed by grace and charity; faith has its own form, while grace gives merit and charity orders it to the supreme good.
Faith concerns what is above reason and has an affective certainty exceeding demonstration.
Faith is the foundation of the spiritual life and naturally prior to the other virtues.

alalal-z20277.summary: Distinction 24 of Book III answers objections to the claim that faith concerns things not seen, and develops a full account of the articles of faith and the creeds. Faith has no merit where reason gives proof. Reasons can induce and ease assent but never cause it, and proof is needed only that the revealer is truthful. Faith's praise lies in assenting to what is above reason, not against it, and faith corrects reason as darkened by phantasms. The substance of faith, vision of truth, remains in heaven while its enigmatic mode passes away. An article is an indivisible truth about God that constrains us to believe, with divine truth as the efficient, final and formal cause of assent. It is a complex reality ordered to all times, not a time-bound proposition. Albert explains the twelve articles of the Apostles' Creed, one from each Apostle, and the fourteen of the Nicene division, seven on the divinity and seven on the incarnation. Articles were joined or divided to match the number of the Apostles and to exclude heresies, and the Nicene expansions answer specific heresies. The Apostles' Creed is the exemplar, and the pope with a council may make explicit what it contains implicitly without creating a new article. Faith is structured like a science: God's existence and Scripture's truth are its axioms, the articles its conclusions, and moral truths its corollaries. Faith and science can concern the same thing in different respects. Credibles are of three kinds: canonical history, truths accessible to reason, and truths beyond reason. There is an experiential knowledge of God beyond faith and short of vision, and faith comes from hearing because it is received from a higher source.
claims: Reasons can induce but never cause the assent of faith, which is meritorious because it rests on what is above reason.
An article of faith is an indivisible truth about God, a complex reality ordered to all times, which constrains belief.
The Apostles' Creed has twelve articles and the Nicene division fourteen; later creeds explain the Apostles' Creed against heresies, and the Church can make implicit articles explicit.
Faith is structured like a science, with axioms, articles as conclusions, and moral corollaries.
Faith and rational science can concern the same thing in different respects.

alalal-z20466.summary: Distinction 25 of Book III treats faith in relation to believers: its growth, its sufficiency and certainty, the explicit faith required of different people in different times, and the equality of the theological virtues. Faith grows in the believer's understanding and affection, not in itself or in the number of its articles, which first truth fixes; what grew historically was their explanation. Since the fall, salvation has always required faith in the mediator, at least universally. Explicit faith in the particular mysteries was required only of those who received revelation or instruction, and God provides the necessary revelation to all who do what lies in them. No falsehood can underlie faith, whose truths are immutable by a necessity of order though contingent in themselves. Human expectations such as Abraham's are opinion, not faith. The simple are bound to explicit faith only so far as they have been taught. Implicit faith means disbelieving no article, and heresy lies in pertinacity, not ignorance. Believers misled by a pastor should hold to the Church's common faith. Faith is equal across articles in subject, motive and end, but greater in articles more contrary to reason, and the real presence falls under the article of the passion. The nativity, death, resurrection and judgment of the redeemer form the logical sequence of redemption and must now be believed explicitly by established Christians. Albert denies that John the Baptist doubted Christ's descent into hell. Cornelius believed in the incarnation explicitly and needed only to learn that it had already happened. Faith, hope and charity are equal as habits united in grace, and acts are equal in merit relative to the grace that informs them.
claims: Faith grows in the believer, not in the number of its articles.
Since the fall, salvation has required at least universal faith in the mediator, and God gives sufficient revelation to all who do what lies in them.
No falsehood can underlie faith; its truths are immutable by necessity of order.
The simple are bound to explicit faith only so far as they have been taught; heresy is pertinacity, not ignorance.
Faith, hope and charity are equal as habits united in grace.

alalal-z10001.summary: Partial summary of Book I, based only on the Prologue and Distinction 37 (2 of its 50 direct children; the Praefatio and the other 47 distinctions are not yet interpreted). In the Prologue, Albert expounds Lombard's prologue as an account of the causes of the Sentences. The work is moved by love of God and neighbour against the detraction of heretics. Its matter is the testimonies of faith grounded in first truth, its form is four books proceeding by authority and likeness, and its end is the profession of faith, which by itself refutes heresy. Along the way Albert holds that reason aided by faith reaches what exceeds it, that truth is per se delightful, and that authority is truth found by reason and written down. Distinction 37 treats God's presence in creatures. God is everywhere by essence, presence and power, conserving all things immediately without displacing created causality. He is present to the saints by grace and to Christ by union, and contains rather than is contained by place. Against this, Albert analyses the definitive location and discrete, instantaneous motion of angels, and adds arguments for divine immutability and against the numerical unity of knowledge.
claims: Lombard's work has the testimonies of faith as its matter and the profession of faith as its end, refuting heresy by manifesting truth.
God is present everywhere by essence, presence and power, conserving creatures immediately and grounding their own causality.
Angels are definitively located and move in discrete instants by a power that overcomes distance.

alalal-z10570.summary: Partial summary of Book II, based only on Distinction 44 (1 of its 45 direct children). That distinction closes Book II's treatise on sin. The power of sinning is a real power from God, but it is ordered to evil by the creature's origin from nothing, and only the will commands sin. It then sets out the limits of obedience: authority is never to be obeyed in commanding sin, a higher authority prevails over one derived from it, and the devil and usurped tyrannical power may be resisted, though divine scourges are to be endured. The rest of Book II, including its treatment of creation, angels, the human condition, grace and sin, is not covered here.
claims: The power of sinning is from God as a power but ordered to evil from the creature's nothingness.
Obedience is bounded: no authority binds to sin, and usurped power may be resisted.

alalal-z15805.summary: Partial summary of Book III, based only on Distinctions 23 to 25, the treatise on faith (3 of its 41 direct children; the Christology and the treatises on hope, charity, the other virtues, the gifts and the commandments are not covered). Albert presents faith as a theological virtue in the affective intellect. Its assent is moved by the will and grounded in first truth, not in evidence, so it is more certain than demonstration while concerning what is above reason. Faith is one in its formal object and many in its articles. Unformed faith becomes formed by grace and charity, and faith is the foundation of the spiritual life, prior to the other virtues. The articles are indivisible truths about God, numbered twelve in the Apostles' Creed and fourteen in the Nicene division. Later creeds explain the Apostles' Creed against heresies, and the Church may make explicit what is implicit. Faith grows in the believer, not in its articles. Since the fall salvation has required faith in the mediator, explicit as far as each person has been taught. Heresy lies in pertinacity, and faith, hope and charity are equal as habits in grace.
claims: Faith is a theological virtue whose assent rests on first truth through the will, not on evidence, and is more certain than demonstration.
The articles of faith are indivisible truths about God, fixed by first truth and explained but not increased by the creeds.
Explicit faith is required according to what one has been taught; implicit faith means disbelieving no article.

alalal.summary: Partial summary of Albert the Great's Commentary on the Sentences, based only on partial summaries of Books I, II and III (3 of 4 books have any interpreted content, and each is itself partial; Book IV is not covered). The covered sections are the exposition of Lombard's prologue and Distinctions I.37, II.44 and III.23 to 25. In them Albert treats theology's matter as the testimonies of faith grounded in first truth. He holds that God is present to all things by essence, presence and power, conserving them immediately, and he contrasts this with the definitive location and discrete motion of angels. He explains the power of sinning as a power from God that is ordered to evil by the creature's nothingness, and he sets limits to obedience. Across three distinctions he develops a full account of faith as a theological virtue whose will-moved assent to first truth exceeds demonstration, together with its articles, creeds, growth, and the explicit faith required of different believers. Throughout, he combines Aristotelian natural philosophy with patristic authority, while rejecting Averroist and other philosophical positions where they conflict with faith. These sections do not represent the work as a whole.
claims: Theology rests on the testimonies of faith grounded in first truth, which reason aided by faith can approach.
God is present to all creatures by essence, presence and power, conserving them immediately.
Faith is a theological virtue whose will-moved assent to first truth exceeds the certainty of demonstration.
